title: Transformers and LLMs from Scratch
premise: The flagship of Block II, and the largest course in the programme. It ends with a working GPT you can explain line by line — from the byte-pair tokeniser you wrote through to the sampler — which is the single most legible artifact this degree produces. The thing being bought is not the ability to build one; nanoGPT already exists. It is that after this, every architectural claim in a paper or a vendor's release notes is checkable against something you have implemented rather than taken on trust.
why_here: Eleventh overall, and the first course in the programme where the prerequisite chain is genuinely load-bearing: it needs the chain rule from AIE-201, the evaluation discipline from AIE-202, and the autodiff engine and training instrumentation from AIE-203. It is also the course that makes a capability claimable — until it is done, 'Transformer architecture' is not a line this transcript can support.
laboratory: 1 Percent More Fluent, for the half of this course nobody expects. It carries text in several languages, and the same sentence costs wildly different numbers of tokens depending on which — a real, measurable cost and latency problem sitting inside a product you already run. The tokeniser module is not an academic exercise there; it is the explanation for a bill.
sitting_rule: Every item is completable in one sitting. Nothing exceeds 180 minutes, and anything over 90 declares its own checkpoints.
honesty_note: No advanced standing. Using an LLM API daily for two years evidences nothing about attention, and the portfolio contains no implementation of any component of one.

panel.blind_note: Judges see the submission and the rubric, never each other's scores, and never the learner's self-assessment.
panel.disagreement: Scores are reported per judge and never averaged into a single number when the spread is 2 or more on any criterion.
panel.bias_warning: The judges are transformers being asked to assess an implementation of a transformer, and they have memorised nanoGPT. They are instructed to score against the rubric and the submitted code rather than against how closely it resembles the reference, and to treat a deliberate, explained divergence as evidence of understanding rather than as an error.

modules.title: Tokenisation, which is where the bill comes from

items.title: Building a byte-pair encoder
items.locator: The tokenizer video — building BPE from scratch, and the section on why so many model failures are really tokeniser failures.

items.title: The three tokenisation algorithms in use
items.locator: The tokenizers chapters — byte-pair encoding, WordPiece and Unigram, and the section on training a new tokeniser from an old one.

items.title: Byte-pair encoding from scratch
checkpoints: Merge training loop implemented over a real corpus
Encode and decode round-trip verified on held-out text
Vocabulary size varied and compression measured
Compared against a reference tokeniser on the same text
items.brief: Implement byte-pair encoding: the merge-training loop, the encoder and the decoder. Train it on a corpus of your own. Verify that encode-then-decode is the identity on held-out text including punctuation, emoji and whitespace runs — that is where naive implementations quietly lose bytes. Then vary the vocabulary size and measure compression, so the trade between vocabulary and sequence length is a curve you have seen rather than a claim you have read.

items.title: What your tokeniser costs in every language
checkpoints: The same content prepared in several languages
Token counts measured per language with a production tokeniser
Cost and context consequences computed at a real price
A mitigation considered and its trade stated
items.brief: Take the same passage in every language 1 Percent More Fluent supports and measure how many tokens each becomes under the tokeniser you actually pay for. Convert that into money at the real per-token price and into context-window consumption. The ratio between the cheapest and the most expensive language will be larger than you expect, and it is a fact about your product's economics, not a curiosity. Finish by naming one thing you could do about it and what it would cost.

items.title: Attention Is All You Need, in full
items.locator: Sections 3 and 4 entirely. AIE-201 read only 3.2.1, for the scaling argument; this is the rest of the architecture, including why multi-head exists at all.

items.title: Let's build GPT: the attention half
items.locator: Through the self-attention sections — the mathematical trick with the triangular mask, then single and multi-head attention.

items.title: Multi-head self-attention, from scratch
checkpoints: Single-head attention implemented and shape-checked
Causal mask applied and verified to block future positions
Extended to multi-head with heads genuinely independent
Output matched against torch.nn.MultiheadAttention on identical weights
items.brief: Implement scaled dot-product attention, then causal masking, then multi-head — without opening a reference. Verify the mask does what you think by feeding a sequence where a leak would change the output at position zero. Then load identical weights into torch.nn.MultiheadAttention and confirm your output matches to a stated tolerance. The weight-loading step is the assignment: matching on random weights proves nothing, and getting the layout right is where the understanding is.

items.title: What the heads are actually doing
checkpoints: Attention weights extracted per head per layer
Visualised over real input
One head given a defensible description
One head reported as not interpretable
items.brief: Extract and visualise attention weights from a small trained model across heads and layers. Find one head whose behaviour you can describe defensibly — attending to the previous token, to a matching delimiter, to the subject of the sentence — and evidence it across several inputs rather than one. Then find a head you cannot characterise and say so. The second half is the assignment: attention maps are famously easy to over-read, and a submission where every head has a tidy story is a submission that invented some.

items.title: Self-attention in the NLP lineage
items.locator: The self-attention and transformers lectures — attention as it arrived from sequence-to-sequence models, which is the context the paper assumes.

modules.title: A GPT you can explain line by line

items.title: Let's build GPT: assembling the model
items.locator: The remainder — blocks, residual connections, layer normalisation placement, and the training loop.

items.title: Build the model
checkpoints: Token and position embeddings, blocks, and output head assembled
Parameter count computed by hand and matched
Trained on a small corpus with the loss falling
Text generated that is recognisably from the training distribution
items.brief: Assemble the full model from your attention implementation: embeddings, stacked blocks with residuals and normalisation, and a language-modelling head. Compute the parameter count by hand from the dimensions before asking the framework, and reconcile any difference. Train it on a small corpus until it produces text that is recognisably from that distribution. It will be bad text; that is fine and expected at this scale.

items.title: Sampling is a design decision
checkpoints: Greedy, temperature, top-k and nucleus sampling implemented
Each run on identical prompts and seeds
A quantitative measure of diversity and repetition reported
A recommendation made for one of your own products
items.brief: Implement greedy decoding, temperature scaling, top-k and nucleus sampling on your own model. Run them on identical prompts with identical seeds and measure — repetition rate and distinct-n, not just how the output reads. Then connect it back: your shipped products set these parameters, probably to whatever the default was. Say what you would now set them to and why. This is the item where a from-scratch exercise pays a dividend in production.

items.title: Building an LLM, the book-length treatment
items.locator: The chapters on coding the attention mechanism and on implementing a GPT model from scratch — read after your own implementation exists, as a check on it rather than as instructions.

items.title: Retention: the decoder stack, component by component
Decoder-only architectures and their variants
items.locator: The lectures covering decoder-only models and the architectural changes that separate a modern model from the 2017 paper.

items.title: Three modern components, measured one at a time
checkpoints: Baseline model fixed and its result recorded
RMSNorm substituted and measured
A gated feed-forward substituted and measured
Rotary position embeddings substituted and measured
Parameter counts reconciled across variants
items.brief: Take your working model as the 2017 baseline and substitute three modern components one at a time: RMSNorm for LayerNorm, a gated feed-forward such as SwiGLU for the standard one, and rotary position embeddings for learned ones. Measure each independently, holding parameter count roughly constant. Report which earned its place at your scale and which did not. Modern models use all three; at a few million parameters on a laptop you may find one of them does nothing, and reporting that honestly is worth more than reproducing the expected ordering.

items.title: The engineering decisions in a modern stack
items.locator: The lectures on architecture variants and on the systems decisions behind training a language model — attribution note: cite the course playlist, since the individually reuploaded copies are not authorised.

items.title: A KV cache, and what it buys
checkpoints: Cache implemented for incremental decoding
Output verified identical to the uncached path
Time per token measured with and without, across sequence lengths
items.brief: Add a key-value cache to your model's generation path. First prove it is correct: cached and uncached generation must produce identical tokens for the same seed, and if they do not, the bug is subtle and worth finding. Then measure time per generated token with and without, across several sequence lengths, and state the complexity you have changed and the memory you have traded for it.

items.title: nanoGPT as the reference
items.locator: model.py and train.py — read only after your own implementation exists, and read for the decisions rather than the syntax.

items.title: The reproduction: run it
checkpoints: A published number chosen as the target, with its source cited
The scale you can actually afford stated in advance
The run completed and its result recorded
Compute and wall-clock cost accounted for
items.brief: Pick a published result you can attempt at a scale you can afford — a validation loss on a named dataset at a named parameter count. State the target and your scale before starting. Run it. Record what you got, what it cost in compute and wall-clock, and every deviation from the published setup you had to make. Failing to hit the number is an expected outcome; not knowing why is the failure.

items.title: The reproduction: account for the gap
checkpoints: Every deviation from the published setup enumerated
Each one's likely direction and rough magnitude estimated
The estimates summed and compared against the observed gap
The residual stated as unexplained
items.brief: Enumerate every way your run differed from the published one — data, tokeniser, sequence length, batch size, schedule, precision, training tokens. For each, estimate the direction and rough size of its effect. Add them up and compare against the gap you actually observed. What is left over is the part you cannot explain, and stating it plainly is the point of the exercise. A gap analysis that exactly accounts for the difference is almost always a gap analysis that was fitted to it.

items.title: minGPT, for what it leaves out
items.locator: model.py — the minimal version, read specifically for what it omits relative to nanoGPT and why that is acceptable in a teaching implementation.

items.title: Retention: reproduction and its failure modes
The annotated implementation, published
checkpoints: Repository public, with a README that states what it is and is not
Every non-obvious line carrying a comment that says why
Runnable end to end from a clean checkout
A stated relationship to nanoGPT and minGPT
items.brief: Publish your implementation as a public repository. It must run end to end from a clean checkout on a laptop, and its README must say plainly what it is for and what it is not — it is not a better nanoGPT and should not claim to be. The value is the annotation: every non-obvious line explains why it is there, which is the artifact that distinguishes having built one from having copied one.

items.title: Every choice, and what it buys
checkpoints: Each architectural decision listed with its alternative
Measurements cited where they exist
Choices with no measurement marked as inherited rather than justified
Published and connected backwards to an earlier chapter
items.brief: Write the chapter that goes with the repository: every architectural decision, its alternative, and what choosing it bought. Where you measured, cite the measurement. Where you inherited a choice because everyone does it, say so and mark it as unjustified rather than dressing it up. That distinction — measured versus inherited — is the most useful thing this document can contain, and almost no published write-up makes it.

items.title: Transformer variants and efficiency, a second lineage
items.locator: The lectures on transformer variants and on efficiency — a different teaching tradition from the Stanford lineage, useful for the places the two disagree.

items.title: Read a new architecture cold
checkpoints: A model released after this course was written, chosen
Its architecture section read and summarised
Differences from your implementation enumerated
One difference explained mechanically, not just named
items.brief: Take a model card or technical report published after this course was registered, and read its architecture section cold. Enumerate what differs from what you built. Then pick the one that matters most and explain what it is mechanically doing and what problem it solves — not what the report says it does, but what you can work out from your own implementation. This is the outcome the whole course exists to produce, and it is the only item that uses material nobody could have prepared you for.

items.title: Oral defense
items.brief: Three unscripted questions generated from your own implementation and write-up at defense time, answered aloud without notes and without the code open. This is the defense that carries the transformers capability claim, so it is the one that matters most on a CV.
sample_question_shapes: Open your model file mentally and walk me from a token id to a logit. Where does the residual stream get written to, and by what?
You said RoPE made no measurable difference at your scale. At what scale would you expect it to, and why that scale?
Your reproduction missed the published number by a margin you partly explained. A reviewer says the unexplained residual means your implementation is wrong. Answer them.

rubrics.integrity: This defense carries the transformers capability claim. Judges are instructed that inventing a plausible mechanism under pressure is the single most damaging thing a candidate can do here, and scores criterion 3 at 0.

completion.required: All eight assignments, all four project parts and the defense submitted. Readings and lectures are tier 0 and are tracked but never counted toward mastery.
completion.grade_rollup: Deterministic. Each item's tier sets its weight; panel scores enter as per-criterion values; nothing is rounded up. Computed in TypeScript, never by a model.
completion.mastery_note: Sets initial mastery on all three transformer skills and on tokenisation, and is the course that makes the Transformer architecture capability claimable at all. FSRS then decays them — and for this claim specifically, the cold-recall requirement is the one that matters, because an implementation you cannot walk from memory six months later is a repository rather than a skill.
